units.label: BVF概率测量与扩展
units.description: 模型×职业×上下文×属性类的条件概率；上下文和职业两层汇总，含种族/主题/来源/语言扩展。

units.label: 数学参考与示例
units.description: 三种理想化参照及假设反例，辅助解释主测量，不充当独立训练实验。

units.label: 规模与既有BASE/CHAT比较
units.description: 比较GPT家族规模及Llama2既有版本，未隔离所有训练差异。

units.label: 职业风险社会关联和分布分析
units.description: 职业层面WLS、正态拟合及波动插值描述。

facts.statement: BVF把同一职业在不同文本上下文的刻板倾向分布分解为平均系统偏向与跨上下文波动；研究的是条件token概率的变化，并非已采样自由回答的错误率。

method_function.text: 界定测量构念和概率测量对象。

facts.statement: 基本测量单元是模型M×职业x×上下文c×属性类y；先在C上汇总职业风险，再在X上汇总模型风险。正文比较12个既有模型，数学参考模型另列，不作为新训练模型。

method_function.text: 保留测量、聚合与比较层级。

facts.statement: X为附录D.1完整职业词表，计算整体风险时对职业用均匀分布；Y采用既有属性词表，性别为二类、种族为五类。职业人口数来自劳工统计，但仅用于后续社会因素回归加权。

method_function.text: 区分主风险分母权重与回归权重。

facts.statement: 从HuggingFace clean Wikipedia随机抽10000篇文章；过滤无Y词句，仅留性别词与主语共指或修饰主语的句子，主语随后换成职业。因同时含X和Y的句子太少，实际放宽了必须同时出现两类词的约束。

method_function.text: 构建真实语料上下文并记录实际放宽。

facts.statement: 抽取两个关键词之间谓词，不限制长度；统一过去时、报告动词补that以合并says/said/said that等结构，构成The [X]…[Y]模板。每模板C权重为Count(c)/Σ_C Count(c)，不是等权模板平均。

method_function.text: 规范化模板并确定上下文加权分母。

facts.statement: PDF仅给频数最高的各10个性别/种族模板，完整其余模板指向代码；如性别said that为2142次、felt为105次。种族模板另按职业主语修饰语抽谓词，并把Y移至句尾以适配自回归预测。

method_function.text: 说明可见材料范围及种族特定模板操作。

facts.statement: 对同一属性类的候选词token概率求和，再除以所有属性类并集词的token概率和，得到p_M(y|x,c)（式8）；将其代入式1，并以未指定形式的非参数方法描述跨上下文刻板倾向分布。

method_function.text: 从词概率构造类概率和分布。

facts.statement: 式1定义s=p_M/p*−1；上下文不含属性信息时p*=1/|Y|，二元性别各0.5。s正为刻板、负为反刻板，绝对值为强度。

method_function.text: 明确公平参考和尺度方向。

facts.statement: 风险准则J(s)=max_y max(s_y,0)，职业总体风险r_x=E_C[J(s)]，模型风险R=E_X[r_x]；取正部用以避免反刻板抵消。

method_function.text: 给出最大正偏向及两层聚合。

facts.statement: 偏向风险r_x^b=J(E_C[s])，波动风险r_x^v=r_x−r_x^b；R^b/R^v再分别对X求期望。波动是此分解余量，不是方差或重复生成标准差。

method_function.text: 区分先平均后取J与先取J后平均。

facts.statement: 附录B.1讨论可替代l^k范数与风险厌恶，但明确本文全部结果采用正部向量的l∞范数。

method_function.text: 限定实际准则与仅讨论的替代方案。

facts.statement: 用三个理想化数学参考解释量级：理想公平(R,Rb,Rv)=(0,0,0)，固定极端刻板正文/表格为(1,1,0)，上下文随机在两种极端间等概率切换为(1,0,1)；附录固定刻板式15/16与此冲突，保留两种来源。

method_function.text: 提供非经验参照并显式标识冲突。

facts.statement: 附录A以BERT六职业×10个上下文的男性概率热图说明上下文敏感；另以假设M1/M2三上下文例子比较平均偏向与20%归一化偏差，M1/M2并非实际被测LLM。

method_function.text: 区分经验示例与演示性反例。

facts.statement: 主要12模型为OPT-IML30B、Baichuan13B、Llama2 7B、ChatGLM2 6B、T5 220M、BART139M、GPT-2 137M、RoBERTa125M、XLNet117M、BERT110M、distilBERT67M、ALBERT11.8M。

method_function.text: 确定主要模型比较集合。

facts.statement: 性别风险表中T5总风险0.8703、偏向风险0.8691最高；BERT总风险最低而ALBERT偏向风险最低，两种排序并不一致。几乎所有模型（ALBERT除外）总体倾向男性，nurse/stylist/dietitian等为例外。

method_function.text: 保留指标不同导致的排序及方向性结果。

facts.statement: 作者明确实际将Llama2在三来源聚合的社交媒体有害言论Toxicity Data上微调，比较训练前后性别风险；8 GPU，每GPU batch1、梯度累积4、2epochs、学习率1e−5、warmup比例0.2。

method_function.text: 记录确实施行的干预及训练协议。

facts.statement: 毒性语料微调后总体偏向风险上升而波动风险下降（图6）；这是作者实施的前后比较，不意味着所有波动下降都代表公平改善。

method_function.text: 报告干预结果及指标方向。

facts.statement: 规模比较跨GPT-2 137M/335M/812M/1.61B、GPT-Neo1.3B/2.7B、GPT-NeoX20B；作者报告随规模增大偏向总体上升、波动总体下降，跨家族不是只改参数量的受控训练实验。

method_function.text: 限定规模分析实际比较与混杂边界。

facts.statement: 对Llama2的7/13/70B分别比较既有BASE与额外经过SFT+RLHF的CHAT版本；不报告作者自行实施RLHF。

method_function.text: 辨明对照模型来源与训练归属。

facts.statement: 各大小Llama2 CHAT相对BASE的偏向风险较低、波动较高；作者将其解释为RLHF纠偏但未内化真正性别平等，该机制解释没有被单独识别。

method_function.text: 分开观测方向与作者机制解释。

facts.statement: 以职业为散点单位，用职业人口数作权重的WLS回归风险对收入；附录还回归教育年限、招聘比例、职业词频（图15横轴log(word frequency)），因素来自劳工统计及Wikipedia。

method_function.text: 保留关联模型、自变量与权重。

facts.statement: 作者报告职业收入与歧视风险正相关，并推测源自社会经济及性别角色刻板印象；这是职业层面的关联与解释，不是薪资操纵的因果检验。

method_function.text: 限定社会因素结果及因果边界。

facts.statement: 图10/16对职业偏向风险分布拟合正态分布；波动风险则对计算值插值绘线。附录同时给种族分解分布。

method_function.text: 保留实际可见分布呈现操作。

facts.statement: 作者将波动风险称为fat-tailed并讨论难以预测、与大数定律不同；未报告尾指数、拟合优度或此类理论检验，故该论断保留为作者解释。

method_function.text: 避免把分布讨论升级为证实规律。

facts.statement: 种族表2中XLNet总风险最高0.9333，Llama2偏向最高0.9311且波动最低0.0002，BART总风险最低0.4178、偏向最低0.2971而波动最高0.1207。

method_function.text: 保留多维指标结果及相反排序。

facts.statement: 附录将属性扩展到宗教与残障，表3给BERT/GPT2/T5/Llama2四模型的三种风险；宗教6类、残障7个作者标签，均是概率属性集合，不是受试者群体实验。

method_function.text: 区分属性扩展和新增行为样本。

facts.statement: 用webpage、book、conversation、textbook分别挖掘上下文再比较四模型性别风险（表4）；作者称风险量级变化但最高/最低偏向模型排序保持。另按语言重设X/Y并挖新C，报告BERT-Chinese、GPT2-Chinese、llama2-Chinese（表5）。

method_function.text: 记录实际材料来源与中文扩展检验。

facts.statement: 核心概率测量可调用既有模型，但毒性语料实验明确实际微调Llama2，构成训练范围与冻结筛选标准的实质张力；仅记录这一事实，不重筛论文，也不把所有测试模型当作者训练。

method_function.text: 为后续治理解释保留实际训练边界。

facts.statement: 作者说明仅取二元性别、五类种族是为与既有研究一致、便利比较及展示BVF的实用简化，并承认测量框架有盲点、需按评估目的调整；这些属于局限与伦理讨论，没有据此实际实施额外身份覆盖控制。

method_function.text: 界定概念覆盖限制。

facts.statement: 附录E把J改为知识评价的凹函数、扩展视觉/自动驾驶情境作为讨论或未来工作；本文没有开展知识基准或驾驶实验。相关WEAT等嵌入指标也只在相关工作出现。

method_function.text: 排除非本研究实际方法。

• Ideally Fair Model consistently delivers unbiased predictions, achieving indices R, Rb , and

• Stereotyped Model tends to adhere to extreme unipolar stereotypes, reflected in the maximal

• Randomly Stereotyped Model exhibits significant discrimination in a specific context but
displays random behavior across various contexts, whose discrimination is solely attributable
by volatility risk. As a result, it records the maximal R, Rv value, while minimal Rb .

LLMs exhibit inconsistent stereotypes under different contexts. As demonstrated in the probability
heat map (Figure 11), BERT exhibits varied gender predictions for six professions (nurse, stylist,
receptionist, doctor, programmer, and captain) in 10 different sentences. For example, BERT’s
prediction for the profession of stylist ranges from masculine in sentence 0, to feminine in sentence
1. This highlights the potential for LLMs to be affected by contexts and to exhibit inconsistent
stereotypes.

Data Toxicity: Toxic data in the training set is detrimental to the fairness of LLMs. We fine-tuned
Llama2 on toxic data [Davidson et al., 2017, Iyer, 2021, Surge-ai, 2021] and tested the changes in
gender discrimination risk before and after its training, as shown in Figure 6. For specific fine-tuning
settings, please refer to the table in the Appendix D.4. Toxic data reinforces the model’s systemic
bias, leading to an increase in overall bias risk and a decrease in overall volatility risk.

Hyper-parameters for Fine-tuning on Toxicity Data

We utilized the existing Toxicity Data dataset as our training data, which was constructed by aggregating harmful speech found on social media platforms [Davidson et al., 2017, Iyer, 2021, Surge-ai,
2021]. We fine-tune the Llama2 model underwent on an 8-GPU setup, employing a batch size of
1 on each GPU and 4 gradient accumulation steps. Training was conducted over 2 epochs, with a
learning rate set at 1e-5 and a warm-up ratio of 0.2 applied.

Model Size We investigate the effects of scaling of various GPT family model sizes that are
accessible for public querying. This includes GPT-2 models (137M, 335M, 812M, 1.61B), GPT-Neo
(1.3B, 2.7B), and GPT-NeoX (20B). The results was shown in Figure 7. The overall trend shows
there is a positive correlation between bias and model size, indicating that larger models might
be more susceptible to overfitting or capturing biases present in the data. Conversely, volatility
tends to decrease as model size increases, suggesting that larger models exhibit more consistent
discrimination.

RLHF Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) ensures the fairness of LLMs by
aligning the model with human preferences [Stiennon et al., 2020, Ouyang et al., 2022]. We evaluated
the impact of RLHF on model bias under our BVF. We tested three different sizes of LLAMA2 series
models (7b, 13b, 70b) as detailed by Touvron et al. [2023]. This included the BASE models pretrained on text, as well as the chat versions that undergo additional stages of supervised fine-tuning
and RLHF. The results are illustrated in Figure 8.

Figure 8: The impact of RLHF on bias risk and volatility risk.
Our observations indicate that across various sizes of Llama models, the chat versions refined with
RLHF exhibit a lower bias risk compared to the base versions, yet they possess a higher volatility risk.
This suggests that while RLHF is capable of correcting inherent prejudices within the model, it does
not effectively instill the principles of genuine gender equality, resulting in the model’s continued
capricious behavior.

explore the relationship between the model’s occupational discrimination risk and the salary of that
occupation using weighted least squares (WLS), where the weights are the number of people in that

distribution with normal distribution. To better demonstrate the amorphous distribution of volatility
risk, we perform interpolation on the calculated values and plot the interpolated lines.
We compile the distribution of bias risk rxb and volatility risk rxv under gender topic corresponding to
different occupations x, as shown in Figure 10. Bias risk is typically characterized by a distribution
that closely approximates normal distribution, underpinned by the principles of regression to the mean
and the law of large numbers. Conversely, volatility risk is characterized by a fat-tailed distribution,
diverging noticeably from adherence to the law of large numbers and presenting inherent challenges
in precise forecasting, potentially rendering it infeasible. It is crucial to remain vigilant in addressing
such unpredictable risks to prevent any potential loss of control over risk management protocols.

If we employ the average performance, i.e., system bias in this scenario, as a discrimination measure,
this approach overlooks the variation of the entity’s preferences, which reflects inconsistency and
unpredictability in their predictions or decision-making. Such oversight can lead to measurement
outcomes that defy intuitive understanding, as seen in the case of M2 , which exhibits fluctuated
biased preferences across contexts, yet its system bias remains at 0. Furthermore, deviation alone
cannot fully capture the biased behavior of the models. For instance, comparing M1 and M2 , while
both have the same deviation to be 20%, it does not account for the fact that the predictions of
M2 exhibit larger variations, and its preferences are more biased in certain contexts. Consequently,
a comprehensive quantitative measure of model discrimination should i) consider both average
performance and performance variation, termed bias and volatility in our study, respectively; and ii)
facilitate their decomposition accordingly.

Definition of Justice-related Topics In our investigation, we employ a framework predicated on the
utilization of binary gender classification and a 5-category race taxonomy. This selection is made with
the intention of maintaining congruity with previous research, thereby facilitating a clearer comprehension of our discrimination assessment method BVF. It is imperative to underscore, however, that
our adoption of such classifications in no way diminishes our profound respect for individuals whose
identities transcend these conventional delineations. Rather, it serves as a pragmatic methodological
choice aimed at fostering comparability and coherence with existing research paradigms.
Tailored BVF Adjustment for Dedicated Assessment Purposes While we emphasize the theoretical
robustness and broad applicability of the BVF in evaluating the inductive biases inherent within
LLMs, we recognize the need to customize our approach to meet the specific evaluation goals. We
acknowledge that every measurement framework has flaws and blind spots. Therefore, we approach
evaluation with careful methodology, understanding the need for continual improvement to better
grasp fairness and justice in our analysis.

BVF is a statistical framework capable of measuring LLM’s knowledge and stereotypes, where the
transition between these two measurement scenarios mainly depends on how criterion J is defined.
We have mentioned the concept of parametric biases several times in previous sections, indicating the
conditional relationships among words that the LLM learns from its pre-training data, often inferred
from cues like word co-occurrence rates. This represents the LLM’s preliminary comprehension of
the world gleaned from its exposure to vast textual data. People subjectively label inductive biases
that help the LLM accomplish tasks harmlessly as knowledge, seen in its ability to generate statements
like “Pride and Prejudice is authored by Jane Austen,” or “Fubini’s theorem states that the order
of integration doesn’t matter when the integral’s absolute value is finite.” In our work, inductive
biases considered as potentially harmful are labeled as stereotype, such as when the LLM is more
inclined to interpret a demographic group as either victims or criminals, hindering fair judgments,
or when it biases a certain group of people towards certain professions, perpetuating social class
intergenerational transmission.
Our framework was initially designed to measure this broader notion of parametric biases, thus
allowing for the assessment of LLM’s knowledge alongside the stereotype. When J is defined to
evaluate the LLM’s mastery of knowledge, stereotype in this work corresponds to knowledge, while
volatility corresponds to confidence in this knowledge. More specifically, when J is designed as
a concave5 function of model prediction p, according to Jensen’s inequality, E(J(p)) < J(E(p)),
indicating that the overall metric E(J(p)) is less than the performance metric of deterministic
knowledge J(E(p)) under criterion J. The difference in these two terms here stems from the
confidence in knowledge. We leave the refinement of this knowledge measurement framework as
future work.

effectiveness. However, existing evaluation methods for LLMs primarily assess average performance
across test samples, which fails to capture these inconsistencies. For example, the knowledgetesting benchmark MMLU [Hendrycks et al., 2021] only evaluates each concept once with a fix
question prompt, leading to significant variations in models’ test accuracy on any small sub-split
(e.g., astronomy) when the initial task-instructional prompts are slightly modified.
Consequently, we suggest that in model auditing, in addition to the traditional measure of average
task performance, one should also take into account performance variation, indicating inconsistencies
in behavior across various contexts. Indeed, much akin to evaluating human performance across
diverse situations when recruiting labor, we should similarly assess the holistic behavior of models
before grounding them in real-world applications.
E.3

Instantiation of Context C

Expanding the scope of context allows this framework to measure the inductive bias of models across
diverse modalities. In this study, context primarily refers to the textual environment upon which the
LLM is conditioned, while for visual models, such as those in autonomous vehicles determining
steering angles from visual inputs, the context covers all encountered visual scenarios.
Evaluating the inductive biases of models across modalities is equally essential for their safe practical
deployment. For instance, assessing the qualification of a visual model for autonomous vehicles
requires at least measuring its knowledge of traffic-norm related video-action pairs such as <video:
running emergency vehicle, action: yield>, where the videos constitute the major contexts. In
testing this knowledge, visual contexts should encompass not only commonly encountered emergency
vehicles like ambulances and police cars but also ones from the long-tail distribution, such as fire
trucks [Shakir, 2023]. Likewise, determining the applicability of this visual model for autonomous
driving systems also necessitates the evaluation of both the average performance and the performance
variance regarding a set of traffic knowledge of a similar nature.

Related Work

LLMs have been empirically demonstrated to manifest biased tendencies and generation inconsistencies [Crawford, 2017, Bordia and Bowman, 2019, Perez et al., 2022, Gallegos et al., 2024, Yang et al.,
2024]. Numerous studies have aimed to develop methods for quantifying social biases in LLMs,
revealing the models’ inclination towards inequitable or prejudiced treatment of distinct population
groups. Based on the different manifestations of these inequitable or prejudiced treatments, prior
works on bias measurement in LLMs can be categorized into two main types:
Word Embedding Metrics This category of methods quantifies the biases present in LLMs by
examining the geometric properties of their embeddings, such as the distance between neutral terms
9

(e.g., occupations) and identity-related terms (e.g., gender pronouns) in the vector space. Bolukbasi
et al. [2016] were the first to measure bias through the angle between word embeddings. Subsequent
works, such as Caliskan et al. [2017] and Dev et al. [2020], have used cosine similarity between
different word classes to assess model discrimination, inspired by the Implicit Association Test (IAT;
Greenwald et al. 1998), and introduced the Word Embedding Association Test (WEAT) dataset. More
recent studies have extended WEAT to multilingual contexts [Lauscher et al., 2020] and contextual
settings [May et al., 2019, Kurita et al., 2019, Dolci et al., 2023]. However, several reports suggest
that biases identified in the embedding space exhibit only weak or inconsistent correlations with
biases observed in downstream tasks [Cabello et al., 2023, Goldfarb-Tarrant et al., 2020].
Probability-Based Metrics One of the most widely used techniques for measuring biases in LLMs
today is based on statistical metrics. For instance, Nadeem et al. [2020] assess LLM bias by analyzing
how often the model selects stereotype-conforming or stereotype-rejecting choices when provided
with cloze-style inputs. Similarly, Nangia et al. [2020] evaluate bias by examining the distribution
of the model’s scores for stereotype-laden sentences. Statistical metrics are more adaptable to
downstream tasks and have been applied across various NLP tasks such as coreference resolution
[Webster et al., 2018, Zhao et al., 2018, Lu et al., 2020], hate speech detection [Sap et al., 2019],
question answering [Li et al., 2020, Zhao et al., 2021], text classification [De-Arteaga et al., 2019],
and knowledge assessment [Dong et al., 2023, Zhang et al., 2024]. However, current evaluation
methods primarily focus on biases in the model’s probability predictions under specific templates,
without accounting for prediction volatility or the probabilistic nature of the model’s responses.

Due to the diverse and thus challenging-to-enumerate forms of context templates collected from the
corpus, we present only the top ten templates here based on their frequency of occurrence, which
will determine their final weight for aggregation. The remaining templates are released alongside the
code.

Data Toxicity: Toxic data in the training set is detrimental to the fairness of LLMs. We fine-tuned
Llama2 on toxic data [Davidson et al., 2017, Iyer, 2021, Surge-ai, 2021] and tested the changes in
gender discrimination risk before and after its training, as shown in Figure 6. For specific fine-tuning
settings, please refer to the table in the Appendix D.4. Toxic data reinforces the model’s systemic
bias, leading to an increase in overall bias risk and a decrease in overall volatility risk.
Model Size We investigate the effects of scaling of various GPT family model sizes that are
accessible for public querying. This includes GPT-2 models (137M, 335M, 812M, 1.61B), GPT-Neo
(1.3B, 2.7B), and GPT-NeoX (20B). The results was shown in Figure 7. The overall trend shows
there is a positive correlation between bias and model size, indicating that larger models might
be more susceptible to overfitting or capturing biases present in the data. Conversely, volatility
tends to decrease as model size increases, suggesting that larger models exhibit more consistent
discrimination.
